content: 1. Silvia, Julia, and Patti Gravitt are affiliated with the National Cancer Institute in the USA, focusing on global health initiatives in the Americas. Rolando Herrero represents the Costa Rican Agency for Biomedical Research, while Ebony Johnson is a community representative for women living with HIV in the Americas. Mauricio Maza from Basic Health International in El Salvador and Raul Murillo from Hospital Universitario San Ignacio in Colombia also contribute to health efforts in the Americas. Kelle Moley, representing the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, focuses on reproductive health technologies in the USA. Gina Ogilvie from BC Women’s Hospital and Health Centre in Canada, and Maria Alejandra Picconi from the HPV Reference Laboratory in Argentina, are key contributors to cervical cancer research and prevention in the Americas. Leeya Pinder from the University of Washington and Veronica Reis from Jhpiego in the USA also play significant roles in advancing health initiatives in the region. 2. Gracia Violetta Ross from the Bolivian Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS and Vikrant Sahasrabuddhe from the National Cancer Institute in the USA are involved in health advocacy and research in the Americas. Rose Slavkovsky and Kerry Thomson, both from PATH in the USA, contribute to health program development. Nicolas Wentzensen from the National Cancer Institute in the USA focuses on cervical cancer prevention strategies. 3. In the Eastern Mediterranean region, Waqar Muhammad Atif from Aga Khan University Hospital in Pakistan, Ali Ghanbari-Motlagh from the Ministry of Health in Iran, and Tarek Hashem from Menoufia University in Egypt are key figures in advancing cancer research and treatment. 4. In Europe, Laia Bruni from the Catalan Institute of Oncology in Spain, Marie-Claude Boily from Imperial College London, and Joanna Cain from the International Federation of Obstetrics and Gynecology (FIGO) in the UK contribute to cancer prevention and women’s health. Helen Kelly from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, Anne Mackie from Public Health England, and Patrick Petignat from Hôpitaux Universitaires de Genève in Switzerland are involved in screening and quality assurance programs. Walter Prendiville from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in France and Peter Sasieni and Julie Torode from King’s College London are also prominent contributors. 5. In South-East Asia, Neerja Bhatla from the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in India, Wachara Eamratsameekool from Phanomphrai Community Hospital in Thailand, Ashrafun Nessa from Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University in Bangladesh, and Myint Myint Thinn from Central Women’s Hospital in Myanmar are advancing cervical cancer prevention and treatment. 6. In the Western Pacific region, Bayarsaikhan Luvsandorj from the National Cancer Center of Mongolia and Fanghui Zhao from the China Cancer Institute are key contributors to cancer research and prevention. 7. The WHO guidelines emphasize the use of HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method for cervical cancer, rather than visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology, for both the general population and women living with HIV. This recommendation is supported by moderate-certainty evidence and is considered a strong recommendation. 8. For women living with HIV, WHO suggests initiating regular cervical cancer screening at the age of 25, based on low-certainty evidence. Screening can be stopped after the age of 50 if two consecutive negative results are obtained, consistent with recommended intervals. 9. WHO recommends prioritizing screening for women aged 30–49 in the general population, as this age group is at higher risk for cervical cancer. Regular screening intervals of 5–10 years are suggested for the general population, while women living with HIV should be screened every 3–5 years. 10. The guidelines also highlight the importance of transitioning to programs with recommended regular screening intervals. However, even screening twice in a lifetime can provide significant benefits for both the general population and women living with HIV. 11. Dual-stain cytology (p16/Ki-67) is recommended as a triage test following a positive HPV DNA test, with further management determined by colposcopy or histopathology results. This approach is part of a screen, triage, and treat strategy. 12. The guidelines emphasize the need for follow-up testing at 12 months post-treatment for women treated with ablation or LLETZ (large-loop excision of the transformation zone). If results are negative, women can return to routine screening intervals. If positive, further evaluation and management are required. 13. The WHO guidelines provide detailed algorithms for cervical cancer screening and treatment, including the use of HPV DNA and mRNA tests, triage methods, and follow-up protocols. These recommendations aim to improve cervical cancer prevention and management globally, with a focus on evidence-based practices and resource feasibility.
